analogy.p: Think of each amino acid as a train carriage with a **hook at one end (-NH2)** and a **loop at the other (-COOH)**. When two carriages are coupled, a small **bolt (the water molecule)** is removed to let the hook and loop connect, and the join is the **peptide link**. Keep adding carriages and you get a long train: a **polypeptide**. Carriages of different colours (different R groups) in a particular order make a **protein**, and the order decides how the train coils up when stored. The analogy breaks down because a real train's carriages are all identical in shape, while amino acids differ in their R groups, and chemical bonding involves atoms being lost rather than a physical bolt being removed.
analogy.t: A train made of carriages with a coupling at each end

bullets: **Amino acids** have **two different functional groups** in one molecule: an **amine group** (-NH2) and a **carboxyl group** (-COOH).
They react by **condensation polymerisation** to produce **polypeptides**, losing **water** each time two join.
**Different amino acids** can be combined in the same chain to produce **proteins**.
**DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) encodes **genetic instructions** for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.
Most DNA molecules are **two polymer chains** made from **four different monomers called nucleotides**, in the form of a **double helix**.
Other natural polymers important for life: **proteins, starch and cellulose**.
**Not required:** the detailed structure of DNA, starch and cellulose.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This point (AQA 4.7, Organic chemistry, **triple science / Chemistry only**) covers three linked ideas. First, **amino acids** have two different functional groups and join by **condensation polymerisation** to make **polypeptides**. Second, different amino acids can be combined in one chain to make **proteins**. Third, **DNA** is a large molecule essential for life, made of two polymer chains of four different monomers called **nucleotides** in a **double helix**; proteins, starch and cellulose are other natural polymers. You must be able to recognise, describe and write simple equations for these ideas, but the detailed structures of DNA, starch and cellulose are **not required**.

bullets: General formula: **H2N-CHR-COOH**, where **R** is the side group.
The **amine group** is -NH2 (written H2N- at the start of a formula); it is **basic**.
The **carboxyl group** is -COOH; it is the same functional group found in carboxylic acids such as ethanoic acid, and it is **acidic**.
Because there are **two different** functional groups, the molecule can react at **both ends**.
The **R group** is the only part that varies: about **20 different amino acids** are used to build the proteins in living things.
Amino acids are **small molecules** (the monomers); polypeptides and proteins are the **polymers**.
Compare with a polyester: there the two groups on each monomer are the **same** (two -OH or two -COOH); an amino acid has **one of each type** on a single molecule.
core.p: Every amino acid has the same basic skeleton: a central carbon atom bonded to an **amine group (-NH2)**, a **carboxyl group (-COOH)**, a **hydrogen atom** and a variable **R group** (side group). The amine group is basic and the carboxyl group is acidic, so the molecule has **two different functional groups**. This matters because it is the combination of an amine at one end and a carboxyl group at the other that lets each amino acid join to two neighbours, one at each end, and so build a long chain.

bullets: **Glycine:** R = H; formula H2N-CH2-COOH; molecular formula **C2H5NO2**; **Mr = 75** (2x12 + 5x1 + 14 + 2x16 = 75).
**Alanine:** R = CH3; formula H2N-CH(CH3)-COOH; molecular formula **C3H7NO2**; **Mr = 89**.
In the exam, if you are given an unfamiliar amino acid, **find the NH2 and COOH groups first**; whatever else is attached is the R group.
The R group may be a simple hydrocarbon, but it can also contain other groups (for example -OH or even another -COOH); this only affects how the finished protein behaves.
For the equations asked for at GCSE, you will almost always be given **glycine** or told to use a general amino acid with R shown.
core.p: The simplest amino acid is **glycine**, where R is just a hydrogen atom, giving the formula **H2NCH2COOH**. **Alanine** has a methyl group as R, so its formula is **H2NCH(CH3)COOH**. Both have exactly the same amine and carboxyl groups, so they react in exactly the same way; only the side group differs. The spec example uses glycine, so make sure you can write its formula from memory and use it as the model for everything else in this topic.

bullets: **Step 1:** two amino acid molecules line up so that the -COOH of one is next to the -NH2 of the other.
**Step 2:** an **-OH** (from the -COOH) and an **H** (from the -NH2) are lost together as **H2O**.
**Step 3:** a new **C-N bond** forms between the two molecules, creating the **peptide link** -CO-NH-.
**Step 4:** the product (a **dipeptide**) still has a free -NH2 at one end and a free -COOH at the other, so more amino acids can add.
Repeating gives a long chain called a **polypeptide**.
**Condensation** = molecules join + a small molecule is lost. **Polymerisation** = repeated many times to make a polymer.
The **by-product is water** every time a link forms.
core.h: How amino acids join: condensation polymerisation
core.p: When two amino acids react, the **-OH from the carboxyl group** of one molecule and a **-H from the amine group** of the other are removed together as a molecule of **water**. The carbon of the first amino acid and the nitrogen of the second are now bonded directly. This is a **condensation reaction** because two molecules join and a small molecule (water) is lost. Because each amino acid still has a free amine group at one end and a free carboxyl group at the other, the process can repeat again and again, giving **condensation polymerisation**.

bullets: Equation (n glycine): **n H2N-CH2-COOH → (-NH-CH2-CO-)n + n H2O**.
The repeat unit **-NH-CH2-CO-** has the formula C2H3NO and Mr = 57 (24 + 3 + 14 + 16 = 57), which is glycine's Mr 75 minus water 18.
For exactly **2 glycines**: H2N-CH2-COOH + H2N-CH2-COOH → H2N-CH2-CO-NH-CH2-COOH + **H2O**; the product has Mr **132**.
For **n** monomers joined into **one chain**, the number of water molecules lost = **n - 1** (every link loses one).
Draw the repeat unit with **open bonds** (or dashed lines) at each end to show the chain continues.
The two ends of a real chain are different: one end has a free **-NH2**, the other a free **-COOH**.
Mark schemes accept the repeat unit written as -NH-CH2-CO- or in the equivalent form showing the same atoms joined in the same order.
core.p: The spec example is that glycine, H2NCH2COOH, polymerises to produce a polymer with the repeating unit **(-NH-CH2-CO-)n** and water. In words: n glycine molecules react to form one polypeptide chain and **(n - 1) molecules of water**; for a very long chain this is often simplified to n water molecules. The repeating unit is what is left of each glycine once the -OH and -H have been removed, so it contains the N, H, CH2 and CO atoms. Always show the **bonds that continue** at each end of the repeat unit, using brackets and n.

bullets: The **peptide link is -CO-NH-** (a carbon double bonded to oxygen, joined to a nitrogen carrying one hydrogen).
It forms between the **carbon of the carboxyl group** of one amino acid and the **nitrogen of the amine group** of the next.
Number of peptide links in a chain of **n** amino acids = **n - 1**.
**Polyester** link = **ester** (-COO-); **polypeptide** link = **peptide** (-CO-NH-): do not mix them up.
Both are **condensation polymers** and both lose **water**.
The reverse reaction (breaking the peptide links by adding water) is **hydrolysis**; in the body this is protein **digestion**, done by **protease** enzymes.
**Link to other topics:** the same -CO-NH- group appears in nylon, a synthetic polyamide made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid.
core.p: The new bond group formed when two amino acids join is called the **peptide link** (also called a **peptide bond**), written **-CO-NH-**. It is the amino-acid equivalent of the **ester link** in a polyester (-COO-). The polymer made from amino acids is therefore a **polypeptide**, and in chemical terms it is a type of **polyamide** because the link is an amide group. A chain made of two amino acids is a **dipeptide**, three a tripeptide, and many a polypeptide.

bullets: A **protein** is a polymer made of **many amino acids** joined by **peptide links**, often with **different** amino acids in the chain.
The **order (sequence)** of amino acids decides how the chain **folds**.
The folded **3D shape** is essential to the protein's function (for example the **active site** of an enzyme must be the right shape for its substrate).
Examples of proteins: **enzymes**, **haemoglobin** (carries oxygen), **antibodies**, **keratin** (hair and nails), **collagen** and **muscle** proteins.
Changing even one amino acid can change the shape and stop a protein working.
DNA carries the instructions that decide the order of amino acids in each protein (link to Biology: protein synthesis).
Proteins are **natural polymers**; the monomers are **amino acids**.
core.p: Living things combine **different amino acids in the same chain**, in a particular order, to produce **proteins**. Because the R groups differ, the chain is not a simple repeat of one unit; instead it is a specific **sequence** of different amino acids. The R groups attract and repel each other, so the long chain folds up into a specific **three-dimensional shape**, and that shape decides what the protein can do. A different sequence means a different shape and therefore a different job.

bullets: **DNA = deoxyribonucleic acid**: know the full name and abbreviation.
It **encodes genetic instructions** for **development and functioning** of living organisms **and viruses**.
It is a **very large molecule** (a polymer), so it has a high relative molecular mass.
The code in DNA specifies the **sequence of amino acids** in proteins.
**Link to Biology:** genes are sections of DNA; the genome is all of an organism's DNA; mutations are changes to the sequence.
Remember that the spec explicitly includes **viruses** as well as organisms in its wording.
Examiners may ask you to **state why DNA is described as a polymer**: it is made of many repeating **monomer** units joined in a long chain.
core.h: DNA: what it is and what it does
core.p: **DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid)** is a large molecule essential for life. It **encodes the genetic instructions** for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses. These instructions are the code that cells use to build proteins, so DNA ultimately controls the characteristics of an organism. DNA is found in the **nucleus** of eukaryotic cells (and in the cytoplasm of bacteria), and it is passed on from parents to offspring, which is why it is the basis of inheritance.

bullets: **Two** polymer chains (strands) in each DNA molecule (for most DNA molecules).
The monomers are called **nucleotides**; there are **four different** nucleotides.
The shape is a **double helix** (two chains twisted around each other).
The **sequence** of the four nucleotides along a chain forms the **code** for making proteins.
DNA is a **polymer** because each strand is made of **many repeating monomer units** joined together.
You do **not** need to know the structure of the bases, the sugar-phosphate backbone or how the strands are held together at this level.
Do not say DNA is made of amino acids: that is a **common error**; amino acids make proteins.
core.h: Structure of DNA: nucleotides and the double helix
core.p: Most DNA molecules consist of **two polymer chains**, made from **four different monomers called nucleotides**. The two chains are twisted around each other in the shape of a **double helix**. Each chain is a polymer because it is a long chain made by joining many nucleotide monomers; the four kinds of nucleotide differ from each other (by the base they carry), and the order in which they appear along the chain is the genetic code. The detailed structure of DNA (names of bases, how nucleotides are bonded) is **not required** at GCSE, so concentrate on the key facts.

bullets: **Proteins:** polymers of **amino acids**.
**Starch:** polymer of **glucose (sugar)** monomers; energy store in plants.
**Cellulose:** polymer of **glucose** monomers; gives plant **cell walls** strength.
**DNA:** polymer of **nucleotides**.
All of these are **natural** polymers, made by living organisms, unlike poly(ethene) and polyesters, which are **synthetic**.
Natural polymers are **biodegradable**, which is why they do not build up as waste in the way many synthetic plastics do.
Details of the structure of DNA, starch and cellulose are **not required**.
core.h: Other natural polymers: proteins, starch and cellulose
core.p: The spec lists **proteins, starch and cellulose** as other naturally occurring polymers important for life. Proteins are made from amino acids. Starch and cellulose are both made from sugar (glucose) monomers, but they are used differently: **starch** is the energy store in plants and **cellulose** is the main structural material in plant cell walls. The detailed structures of starch and cellulose are **not required**, so you only need to know that they are natural polymers made by joining many small monomers.

bullets: **Addition:** monomer has **C=C**; **one product** (the polymer); all atoms of the monomer end up in the polymer.
**Condensation:** monomers have **two functional groups**; **two products** (polymer + small molecule, usually water).
Addition polymer backbone is a chain of **carbon atoms**; condensation polymer backbone contains **ester or peptide links**.
**Polyester:** two **different** monomers (diol + dicarboxylic acid), each with **two identical** groups.
**Polypeptide:** **one type** of monomer **molecule** with **two different** groups (or many different amino acids).
Both types produce **long chain molecules** through **repeated** reactions.
Mass is **not** conserved within the polymer for condensation: the polymer's mass is less than the monomers' total because **water is lost**.
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare the two types of polymerisation, so build a clear comparison. Addition polymerisation (spec 4.7.3.1) uses monomers with a **C=C double bond** and forms **only one product**, the polymer. Condensation polymerisation uses monomers with **two functional groups** and forms a polymer **plus a small molecule** such as water. Amino acids are a special case of condensation monomers because the two functional groups on each molecule are **different**.

bullets: **Dipeptide Mr** = sum of Mr of the two amino acids - 18. Two glycines: 75 + 75 - 18 = **132**.
**Chain of n amino acids** = (n x Mr of monomer) - ((n - 1) x 18).
**Repeat unit Mr** (glycine) = 75 - 18 = **57**.
Check the answer: the polymer's Mr must be **less than** n x Mr of the monomer.
**Mass of water produced**: for n monomers, (n - 1) x 18 g per mole of chains formed.
core.h: Calculations with amino acids and polypeptides
core.p: Calculation questions test whether you appreciate that **water is lost** with every peptide link. To find the relative formula mass of a dipeptide or polypeptide, add up the **Mr of all the amino acids** and then **subtract 18** (the Mr of water) for **each peptide link formed**. Remember that a chain of n amino acids has **n - 1** links. Always show the working: examiners award marks for the correct Mr of the monomer, for subtracting the correct number of waters, and for the final answer.

bullets: **Digestion:** protease enzymes break peptide links by **hydrolysis** (adding water), giving amino acids.
**Enzymes** are proteins; their **shape** depends on the amino acid sequence.
**Protein synthesis:** DNA's code decides the order in which amino acids are joined.
**Polymers:** biodegradable natural polymers contrast with non-biodegradable synthetic ones.
**Functional groups** in Chemistry: -OH (alcohols), -COOH (carboxylic acids), -NH2 (amines), -COO- (esters), -CO-NH- (amides/peptide links).
Questions may ask for a **diagram** of the repeat unit, a **word equation**, or a **comparison** with polyesters.
Always use the words **monomer, polymer, condensation, water, peptide link** where relevant.
core.h: Link to other topics and exam context
core.p: This topic connects several areas of the course. In Biology, proteins, enzymes, digestion, protein synthesis and DNA all rely on the ideas above. In Chemistry, it extends polymer chemistry from addition polymers and polyesters, and it reinforces the idea of **functional groups** (amine, carboxyl, ester, amide). Questions may appear on **Paper 2** (organic chemistry) and often link to an unfamiliar monomer, so practise applying the method to new structures. Since this is **Chemistry only (triple)** content, combined science students do not need it.

exam: **Command word 'Name' (1 mark):** give the exact term, for example **peptide link**, **polypeptide**, **nucleotide** or **double helix**.
**'Give the formula of glycine' (1 mark):** H2NCH2COOH (or H2N-CH2-COOH); both functional groups must be shown.
**'What type of reaction is this?' (1 mark):** **condensation polymerisation** (not just 'polymerisation').
**'What is the other product?' (1 mark):** **water** (H2O); an easy mark often missed.
**'Draw the repeat unit' (2 marks):** one mark for the correct atoms in the correct order, one mark for the **open bonds at each end** (-NH-CH2-CO-).
**'Describe how amino acids form a polypeptide' (3 marks):** (1) the -COOH of one reacts with the -NH2 of another, (2) water is lost, (3) a peptide link forms and the process repeats.

**'Compare condensation and addition polymerisation' (4 marks):** state monomer feature (C=C vs two functional groups), number of products, small molecule lost, and an example of each; use comparative words such as **whereas**.
**'Describe the structure of DNA' (2 to 3 marks):** two polymer chains, four different nucleotides (monomers), double helix.
**'Explain why proteins are polymers' (2 marks):** they are made of many **monomers** (amino acids) joined together in a long chain by peptide links.
**Calculation (3 marks):** show Mr of each amino acid, subtract **18 for each water lost**, and give a final answer; do not forget the number of waters is **one fewer** than the number of monomers.
**Spelling:** write **peptide**, **nucleotide**, **condensation** and **polymerisation** correctly; marks can be lost for ambiguous spellings.

mistakes.r: Nucleotides are the monomers of DNA. Amino acids are the monomers of proteins.
mistakes.w: Amino acids are the monomers of DNA.

mistakes.r: It also produces a small molecule, usually water, every time two monomers join.
mistakes.w: Condensation polymerisation only produces the polymer.

mistakes.r: An amino acid has two different groups: an amine (-NH2) and a carboxyl (-COOH).
mistakes.w: An amino acid has two identical functional groups.

mistakes.r: The peptide link is -CO-NH-; the ester link -COO- is in polyesters.
mistakes.w: The peptide link is -COO- (that is the ester link).

mistakes.r: The repeat unit is -NH-CH2-CO-, because an OH and an H have been lost when each link forms.
mistakes.w: Glycine's polymer repeat unit is just H2NCH2COOH.

mistakes.r: Exactly (n - 1) molecules of water are lost, one per peptide link.
mistakes.w: A chain of n amino acids loses n molecules of water.

mistakes.r: Proteins contain many different amino acids in a specific order, which controls the 3D shape.
mistakes.w: Proteins all contain the same amino acid repeated.

mistakes.r: Most DNA molecules are two polymer chains twisted in a double helix.
mistakes.w: DNA is a single long chain.

mistakes.r: They are natural polymers made from sugar (glucose) monomers.
mistakes.w: Starch and cellulose are made from amino acids.

mistakes.r: Addition polymerisation makes only the polymer; condensation polymerisation loses a small molecule.
mistakes.w: Addition polymers lose water as they form.

summary: AQA triple chemistry wants you to know that **amino acids** (with an amine and a carboxyl group) join by **condensation polymerisation**, losing water, to form **polypeptides**, and that different amino acids in one chain make **proteins**. You must also know that **DNA** encodes genetic instructions and is made of two polymer chains of four different **nucleotides** in a **double helix**, and that proteins, starch and cellulose are other natural polymers. It matters because it links organic chemistry to the biology of enzymes, digestion and inheritance.

terms.d: A molecule with two different functional groups: an amine group (-NH2) and a carboxyl group (-COOH), plus an R side group, general formula H2NCHRCOOH.
The functional group -NH2 found in amino acids; it is basic.
The functional group -COOH found in carboxylic acids and amino acids; it is acidic.
The part of an amino acid that varies; it is attached to the central carbon and makes each amino acid different.
The simplest amino acid, H2NCH2COOH, where R is a hydrogen atom.
A reaction in which two molecules join together and a small molecule, such as water, is lost.
The joining of many monomers, each with two functional groups, to make a polymer while losing a small molecule such as water.
The -CO-NH- group formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of another.
A molecule made of two amino acids joined by one peptide link.
A polymer made from many amino acids joined by peptide links.
A polymer made from amino acids, often several different ones, which folds into a specific three-dimensional shape.
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer.
A very large molecule made of many repeating units (monomers) joined together.
A large molecule essential for life that encodes the genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.
One of four different monomers that join to make a DNA polymer chain.
The shape of most DNA molecules: two polymer chains twisted around each other.
A polymer made by living things, for example proteins, starch, cellulose and DNA.
A reaction in which a molecule is broken down by the addition of water, such as the digestion of proteins into amino acids.

worked.ans: (a) condensation; (b) peptide link -CO-NH-; (c) Mr = 132 (the other product is water, Mr 18)
worked.q: Two glycine molecules (H2NCH2COOH) react together. (a) Name the type of reaction. (b) Name the group formed where the molecules join. (c) Calculate the relative formula mass of the product. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16) [4 marks]
steps: (a) Condensation (polymerisation): two molecules join and water is lost.
(b) The link formed is a peptide link, -CO-NH-.
Two glycines = 150; one water is lost: 150 - 18 = 132.

worked.q: A polypeptide chain is made by joining 100 glycine molecules. Calculate (a) the number of water molecules lost and (b) the relative formula mass of the polypeptide. [3 marks]
steps: Number of peptide links = 100 - 1 = 99, so 99 water molecules are lost.

worked.ans: Full-mark answer: amino acids have an -NH2 and a -COOH group. The -COOH of one reacts with the -NH2 of the next and water is lost, forming a peptide link; repeating this is condensation polymerisation and makes a polypeptide. Many different amino acids joined in a set order form a protein that folds into a specific shape. Unlike addition polymerisation, which needs C=C monomers and makes only a polymer, condensation polymerisation uses monomers with two functional groups and produces water as well as the polymer.
worked.q: Describe how amino acids form proteins, and state two differences between this reaction and addition polymerisation. [6 marks]
steps: Each amino acid has an amine group (-NH2) and a carboxyl group (-COOH).
The -COOH of one amino acid reacts with the -NH2 of another; an OH and an H are lost as water and a peptide link (-CO-NH-) forms.
This repeats many times in condensation polymerisation, giving a polypeptide.
Different amino acids in a specific order give a protein, which folds into a particular 3D shape.
Difference 1: addition polymerisation uses monomers with a C=C bond; amino acids have two different functional groups.
Difference 2: addition polymerisation makes only the polymer; condensation polymerisation also makes a small molecule (water).
